title: Python
description: Learn Python step-by-step from scratch. Clean, bullet-pointed, practical lessons designed for modern learners.

lessons.title: Python Intro & Setup
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 What is Python?

  • High-level Language: Easy to read, write, and maintain.
  • Interpreted: Code executes line-by-line without pre-compilation.
  • Created by: Guido van Rossum in 1991.

💡 Key Advantages

  • Simple Syntax: Looks like plain English sentences.
  • Versatile: Used for Web, AI, Data Science, Automation, & Robotics.
  • Huge Ecosystem: Thousands of free libraries available via PIP.

🎯 Real-World Usage

  • YouTube & Instagram: Powering backend APIs & data processing.
  • OpenAI & ChatGPT: Built primarily using Python ML frameworks.

⚠️ Common Mistake

  • ❌ Mistake: Downloading Python without checking "Add Python to PATH".
  • ✅ Fix: Always tick "Add Python to PATH" during installation.

📝 Quick Task

  • Verify Python installation by typing python --version in your terminal.
lessons.codeExample:
# Verify Python installation
import sys
print("Python version:", sys.version)

lessons.title: Python Hello World
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Your First Program

  • print() Function: Displays text or output on the screen.
  • Strings: Text must be wrapped in quotes (single '...' or double "...").

💡 Key Rules

  • Case-Sensitive: Must be lowercase print() (not Print()).
  • Parentheses Required: Function arguments go inside ().

🎯 Real-World Usage

  • Debugging: Printing status messages during code execution.
  • CLI Tools: Displaying prompts & output to terminal users.

⚠️ Common Mistake

  • ❌ Mistake: Print("Hello") -> NameError!
  • ✅ Fix: Always use lowercase print("Hello").

📝 Quick Task

  • Print your name and your favorite programming language on separate lines.
lessons.codeExample:
print("Hello, World!")
print("Welcome to Progrys Knowledge Hub!")

lessons.title: Python Syntax & Indentation
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Python Code Structure

  • No Curly Braces: Unlike C++/Java, Python uses whitespace/indentation.
  • Indentation Rule: 4 spaces (or 1 tab) define a code block.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Block Statements: Used inside if, for, while, and functions.
  • Line Breaks: Each new command starts on a new line (no semicolons needed).

⚠️ Common Mistake

  • ❌ Mistake: Mixing tabs and spaces in the same file.
  • ✅ Fix: Standardize on 4 spaces per indentation level.

📝 Quick Task

  • Fix the indentation error in a block to make it execute smoothly.

lessons.title: Python Comments
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Why Use Comments?

  • Explain Code: Helps you and others understand logic later.
  • Prevent Execution: Temporarily disable code lines while testing.

💡 Comment Types

  • Single-Line: Starts with #.
  • Multi-Line: Uses triple quotes """...""" or multiple # lines.

✅ Best Practice

  • Write comments explaining WHY code does something, not just WHAT it does.

📝 Quick Task

  • Add a single-line comment above a print statement explaining what it outputs.
lessons.codeExample:
# This is a single-line comment
print("Hello") # Inline comment

"""
This is a multi-line
docstring comment.
"""
lessons.tryItDefault:
# Add your comment here
print("Comments are ignored by Python")

lessons.title: Python Variables
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 What is a Variable?

  • Data Containers: Stores values in computer memory.
  • Dynamic Typing: No need to declare data types manually.

💡 Naming Rules

  • Must start with a letter or underscore _.
  • Cannot start with a number.
  • Use snake_case for multi-word names (e.g., user_age).

🎯 Real-World Usage

  • Storing user session data, cart totals, and database records.

⚠️ Common Mistake

  • ❌ Mistake: 2nd_user = "Alice" -> SyntaxError!
  • ✅ Fix: user_2 = "Alice".

📝 Quick Task

  • Create two variables: name and age. Print both variables.
lessons.codeExample:
x = 5
y = "John"
print(x)
print(y)

# Multiple Assignment
a, b, c = "Orange", "Banana", "Cherry"
print(a, b, c)

lessons.title: Python Data Types
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Built-in Data Types

  • Text: str ("Hello")
  • Numeric: int (10), float (10.5), complex (1j)
  • Sequence: list, tuple, range
  • Mapping: dict ({ "name": "John" })
  • Set: set ({ 1, 2, 3 })
  • Boolean: bool (True / False)

💡 Getting Data Type

  • Use the type() function to check any variable's data type.

📝 Quick Task

  • Check the type of x = 3.14 using print(type(x)).
lessons.codeExample:
x = 5
y = "Hello"
z = 20.5
w = True

print(type(x)) # <class 'int'>
print(type(y)) # <class 'str'>
print(type(z)) # <class 'float'>
print(type(w)) # <class 'bool'>

lessons.title: Python Type Casting
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 What is Type Casting?

  • Explicit Conversion: Converting variables from one data type to another.

💡 Casting Functions

  • int(): Converts value to integer.
  • float(): Converts value to floating-point number.
  • str(): Converts value to string.

🎯 Real-World Usage

  • Converting user input from web forms (received as string) into numbers for calculations.

⚠️ Common Mistake

  • ❌ Mistake: int("hello") -> ValueError!
  • ✅ Fix: Only cast strings that contain valid digits.

📝 Quick Task

  • Convert "100" to integer, add 50, and print the result.
lessons.codeExample:
x = int(1)     # x will be 1
y = int(2.8)   # y will be 2
z = int("3")   # z will be 3

a = str(10)    # a will be '10'
b = float("4.2") # b will be 4.2

print(x, y, z, a, b)

lessons.title: Python Strings & F-Strings
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 String Basics

  • Surrounded by single '...' or double "..." quotes.
  • Multi-line Strings: Use triple quotes """...""".
  • Array-Like: Characters accessed via zero-based indexing str[0].

💡 F-Strings (Modern Formatting)

  • Prefix string with f and use curly braces {var} to inject variables.

🎯 Real-World Usage

  • Creating dynamic welcome emails, URL endpoints, and log entries.

📝 Quick Task

  • Create item = "Book" and price = 15. Print an f-string: "The Book costs $15".
lessons.codeExample:
name = "Alice"
age = 22

# F-String Formatting
message = f"My name is {name} and I am {age} years old."
print(message)

# String Methods
print(name.upper()) # ALICE
print(name.lower()) # alice

lessons.title: Python Booleans
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 What are Booleans?

  • Represents one of two values: True or False.
  • Used for condition evaluation in decision-making logic.

💡 Truthy vs Falsy

  • Falsy Values: 0, "" (empty string), None, [], {}, False.
  • Truthy Values: Almost everything else!

📝 Quick Task

  • Evaluate bool(10 > 5) and print the output.
lessons.codeExample:
is_logged_in = True
has_permission = False

print(10 > 9)  # Returns True
print(10 == 9) # Returns False
print(bool("Hello")) # Returns True
print(bool(""))      # Returns False

lessons.title: Python Operators
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Operator Categories

  • Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, // (floor), % (modulo), ** (exponent)
  • Assignment: =, +=, -=, *=
  • Comparison: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=
  • Logical: and, or, not
  • Membership: in, not in

🎯 Real-World Usage

  • Modulo % 2 == 0 checks if numbers are even or odd.

📝 Quick Task

  • Check if "py" in "python" using membership operator.
lessons.codeExample:
x = 10
y = 3

print(x + y)  # 13
print(x // y) # 3 (Floor division)
print(x % y)  # 1 (Modulo)
print(x ** y) # 1000 (Exponent)

print("py" in "python") # True

lessons.title: Python Lists
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 What is a List?

  • Ordered, mutable (changeable), and allows duplicate elements.
  • Created using square brackets [...].

💡 Key Methods

  • append(item): Add item to the end.
  • remove(item): Remove first occurrence of item.
  • pop(index): Remove item at specific index.
  • len(list): Return list size.

📝 Quick Task

  • Create a list of 3 fruits. Append a 4th fruit and print the list.
lessons.codeExample:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("orange")
print(fruits)
print(fruits[0]) # "apple"
print(len(fruits)) # 4

lessons.title: Python Tuples
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 What is a Tuple?

  • Ordered and immutable (cannot be modified after creation).
  • Created using round brackets (...).

💡 Why Use Tuples?

  • Faster performance: Memory-efficient compared to lists.
  • Data Protection: Prevents accidental alteration of fixed values.

📝 Quick Task

  • Create a tuple of GPS coordinates (latitude, longitude) and print it.
lessons.codeExample:
coordinates = (37.7749, -122.4194)
print(coordinates[0]) # 37.7749

# Unpacking Tuple
lat, lng = coordinates
print(f"Lat: {lat}, Lng: {lng}")

lessons.title: Python Dictionaries
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Key-Value Stores

  • Unordered/ordered (Python 3.7+), mutable, mapped by { key: value }.
  • Keys must be unique and immutable (strings/numbers).

💡 Common Operations

  • dict[key]: Retrieve value.
  • dict.get(key, default): Safe retrieval without crashing if key missing.
  • dict.keys(), dict.values(), dict.items().

📝 Quick Task

  • Create a user dict with name and email. Print the email.
lessons.codeExample:
user = {
  "name": "John Doe",
  "role": "Admin",
  "active": True
}

print(user["name"])
user["role"] = "SuperAdmin"
print(user.get("email", "Not Found"))

lessons.title: Python If...Else
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Decision Making

  • if: Executed if condition is True.
  • elif: Tested if previous conditions were False.
  • else: Catches anything not caught by preceding conditions.

💡 Short-Hand Syntax

  • Ternary Operator: x = "Yes" if condition else "No".

📝 Quick Task

  • Write an if statement checking if age >= 18 to print "Adult".

lessons.title: Python While Loops
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Repeat Until Condition Fails

  • Executes a set of statements as long as a condition is True.

💡 Loop Controls

  • break: Stops the loop immediately.
  • continue: Skips current iteration and moves to next.

⚠️ Caution

  • Always update the counter inside the loop to avoid infinite loops!

📝 Quick Task

  • Print numbers from 1 to 5 using a while loop.
lessons.codeExample:
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i += 1

lessons.title: Python For Loops
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Iterating Over Sequences

  • Used for iterating over a list, tuple, dictionary, set, string, or range.

💡 range() Function

  • range(start, stop, step) generates sequence of numbers.

📝 Quick Task

  • Loop through range(1, 6) and print each number squared.
lessons.tryItDefault:
for i in range(3):
    print("Loop step:", i)

lessons.title: Python Functions
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Reusable Code Blocks

  • Defined using the def keyword.
  • Called by typing function name followed by parentheses func().

💡 Parameters & Arguments

  • Parameters: Variables listed in function definition.
  • Return Value: Use return keyword to output data back.

📝 Quick Task

  • Write a function square(n) that returns n * n.
lessons.codeExample:
def greet(name="User"):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

message = greet("Alice")
print(message)

lessons.title: Python Lambda
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Anonymous Functions

  • Small, one-line functions without a formal name.
  • Syntax: lambda arguments : expression.

🎯 Real-World Usage

  • Used as inline callbacks inside map(), filter(), and sorted().

📝 Quick Task

  • Create a lambda function double = lambda x: x * 2 and test it.
lessons.codeExample:
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(5)) # Outputs 10

add = lambda a, b: a + b
print(add(3, 7)) # Outputs 10
lessons.tryItDefault:
multiply = lambda a, b: a * b
print(multiply(4, 5))

lessons.title: Python Classes & OOP
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Object-Oriented Programming

  • Class: Blueprint for creating objects.
  • Object: Instance of a class containing attributes & methods.
  • __init__(): Special constructor method called on instantiation.

💡 Self Parameter

  • self represents the instance of the class accessing attributes.

📝 Quick Task

  • Create a Car class with brand attribute and instantiate it.

lessons.title: Python Try...Except (Error Handling)
lessons.explanationHtml:
📌 Handling Runtime Errors

  • Prevents app crashes when unexpected errors occur.
  • try: Block of code to test for errors.
  • except: Handles the specific error.
  • finally: Executes regardless of outcome.

📝 Quick Task

  • Wrap division by zero in a try...except ZeroDivisionError block.
